families.title: Landscape metrics
families.intro:
The metrics of a **categorical map** (land cover, habitat and not habitat): each cell has a class, a *patch* is a set
of neighbouring cells of one class, and the metrics describe the patches (patch level), the classes (class level) or
the whole map (landscape level). Terraflux computes the metrics of
[landscapemetrics](https://r-spatialecology.github.io/landscapemetrics/) with the same names and the same numbers, and
FRAGSTATS' statistics that package lacks. The names are landscapemetrics' function names (`lsm_c_ca`: the class-level
total area), and the tables that follow list, for each, what it measures, its formula, the call, and the setting of
the application's operators that selects it.

Two settings change many of the numbers: the patches' **connectivity** (`directions`: 8 neighbours, the default, or 4)
and whether the **map's boundary counts as edge** (`count_boundary`). Patches are found with 8 neighbours unless the
card says otherwise; adjacencies (aggregation, contagion) always use the 4 sides of a cell. The map is in metres:
areas are in hectares and edge lengths in metres.
families.example:
import terraflux as tf

field = tf.nlm.gaussian_field(30, 30, resolution=100, autocorr_range=8, nug=0.0, seed=7)
landscape = tf.nlm.classify(field, 3)    # three classes; the cells are 100 m, so one cell is one hectare

metrics.name: Patch area
metrics.range: > 0, up to the area of the map
metrics.what:
The size of each patch: how much ground one habitat fragment, one field or one lake covers. It is the base of
most other metrics (a patch's shape, core and isolation all depend on its size) and, summarised over a class, it
tells whether a class is made of a few large patches or of many small ones.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\), in hectares
symbols.n_i: the number of cells of patch \(i\)
symbols.\\Delta x, \\Delta y: the cell's width and height, in metres (10 000 m² make a hectare)

metrics.use:
Use it to rank patches and to see the size distribution of a class. The mean alone hides that distribution: a
class of one large patch and many single cells has a small mean and a large standard deviation, so read the
summary statistics (below) together, and the median rather than the mean when a few patches dominate.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

Hesselbarth, M. H. K., Sciaini, M., With, K. A., Wiegand, K., & Nowosad, J. (2019). landscapemetrics: an open-source R tool to calculate landscape metrics. *Ecography*, 42(10), 1648-1657. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.04617

metrics.name: Shape index
metrics.range: 1 for a square, larger the more irregular; no upper limit
metrics.what:
How far a patch's outline is from the simplest one, a square. A compact patch has a value near 1; a long, thin or
indented patch has a higher one. It measures complexity of the outline relative to the patch's size, so it can be
compared between large and small patches.

symbols.p_i: the perimeter of patch \(i\), in metres, that is every cell side that faces another class, a hole, a missing cell or the edge of the map
symbols.A_i: the area of patch \(i\), in square metres

metrics.use:
Use it to find elongated or ragged patches (riparian strips, patches cut by roads) and to compare how compact the
patches of two classes are. Very small patches take only a few values (a single cell is exactly 1), so a class of
many tiny patches has a mean close to 1 whatever its shape. In the library, `convention="fragstats"` compares the
perimeter with the smallest possible perimeter of as many cells instead (the raster version of FRAGSTATS).
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total (class) area
metrics.range: > 0, up to the total area of the map
metrics.what:
The area a class covers in the map: how much forest, pasture or water there is, in hectares. It is the simplest
composition measure, and the quantity the next metric turns into a share.

symbols.\\mathrm{CA}_c: the total area of class \(c\), in hectares
symbols.n_c: the number of patches of class \(c\)
symbols.a_{ic}: the area of patch \(i\) of class \(c\), in hectares

metrics.use:
Use it to report the amount of habitat. It says nothing about how that area is arranged: ten hectares in one
block and ten hectares in a hundred scattered cells have the same value. Pair it with the number of patches or an
aggregation metric.

metrics.name: Percentage of landscape
metrics.range: (0, 100]; the classes of a map add up to 100
metrics.what:
The share of the map that a class covers. Unlike the area in hectares it can be compared between maps of different
sizes, so it is the usual way to say how much habitat a landscape has.

symbols.\\mathrm{CA}_c: the area of class \(c\), in hectares
symbols.\\mathrm{TA}: the total area of the map, in hectares, without the missing cells

metrics.use:
Use it for the habitat amount that many thresholds are stated in (a landscape with less than a given share of
habitat tends to lose species faster). The share is of the cells that have a value: missing cells are left out of
the total.

metrics.name: Edge density
metrics.range: 0 or more; 0 when the class has no edge with another class
metrics.what:
How much boundary a class has with other classes, per hectare of map. A class with a lot of edge is cut into
many parts or has convoluted outlines, and a lot of its area lies close to a different land cover.

symbols.\\mathrm{TE}_c: the total edge of class \(c\), in metres, that is the length of every cell side shared with a cell of another class
symbols.\\mathrm{TA}: the total area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Use it to compare how fragmented or exposed a class is in maps of different sizes (the density, unlike the
total edge length, does not grow with the map). By default the map's own boundary and the missing cells are not
counted as edge; with `count_boundary=True` they are. The map must be in metres for the unit to hold.

metrics.name: Aggregation index
metrics.range: 0 to 100; NA for a class of a single cell
metrics.what:
How clumped a class is. It counts the pairs of side-by-side cells that are both of the class (like adjacencies) and
compares them with the most such pairs that many cells could have, which is when they form the most compact block
possible. It is 0 for a class whose cells never touch and 100 for a class in one compact block.

symbols.g_{cc}: the number of pairs of side-by-side cells that both belong to class \(c\), each pair counted once
symbols.\\max g_{cc}: the largest value \(g_{cc}\) could take for a class of \(n_c\) cells, reached by the most compact block
symbols.n_c: the number of cells of class \(c\)
symbols.s, m: the side of the largest square of \(n_c\) cells, and the cells left over

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the clumping of classes that differ in area: unlike a simple count of patches, it is scaled by
what the class's own area allows. It looks at the four sides of each cell, whatever the patches' connectivity.
refs: He, H. S., DeZonia, B. E., & Mladenoff, D. J. (2000). An aggregation index (AI) to quantify spatial patterns of landscapes. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 591-601. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008102521322

metrics.name: Shannon's diversity index
metrics.range: 0 (one class) to ln m for m classes of equal area
metrics.what:
How many classes the map has and how evenly their areas are spread, in one number. It is the Shannon index of
ecology applied to the area shares of the land-cover classes: it grows with the number of classes and, for a given
number, is highest when they cover equal areas.

symbols.p_c: the share of the map covered by class \(c\), that is \(\mathrm{CA}_c / \mathrm{TA}\)
symbols.m: the number of classes present in the map

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the compositional diversity of landscapes. It ignores where the classes are (a map and its
shuffled cells have the same value), and it is sensitive to rare classes. Its largest possible value depends on
the number of classes, so divide by ln m (Shannon's evenness, `lsm_l_shei`) to compare maps with different
numbers of classes. The logarithm is the natural one.
refs: Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. *Bell System Technical Journal*, 27(3), 379-423. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x

metrics.name: Contagion
metrics.range: (0, 100]; NA for a map of one class
metrics.what:
How clumped the classes of the whole map are. Take every pair of side-by-side cells: contagion is high when most of
the pairs are two cells of the same class (a map of a few large patches) and low when classes are mixed up cell by
cell, so that any two neighbours are likely to differ.

symbols.p_{ij}: the share of all pairs of side-by-side cells (counted in both directions) that join a cell of class \(i\) to a cell of class \(j\); a term with \(p_{ij}=0\) is left out
symbols.m: the number of classes present in the map

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the overall grain of landscapes with the same classes. It depends on the number of classes and
on how their areas are shared, so compare it between maps with the same legend. It counts the four sides of each
cell and leaves out edges to missing cells and to the map's boundary.
refs: O'Neill, R. V., Krummel, J. R., Gardner, R. H., Sugihara, G., Jackson, B., DeAngelis, D. L., Milne, B. T., Turner, M. G., Zygmunt, B., Christensen, S. W., Dale, V. H., & Graham, R. L. (1988). Indices of landscape pattern. *Landscape Ecology*, 1(3), 153-162. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00162741

families.title: Surface metrics
families.intro:
The metrics of a **continuous surface**: an elevation model, an NDVI image, a canopy-height model, any raster whose
cells are measurements and not classes. They come from the surface texture parameters of ISO 25178 and the R package
[geodiv](https://cran.r-project.org/package=geodiv), which brought them to landscape ecology as *gradient surface
metrics*. They need no classification into patches. A trend (a slope across the whole map) is usually removed first,
so that the metrics describe the texture and not the tilt: `tf.surface.remove_plane`, or use a map that has had it
removed.

A metric is computed on all the cells with a value, or in a moving window with `tf.surface.window_metrics`. Heights
are in the unit of the raster, and the metrics that are not unitless say so on their card.
families.example:
import terraflux as tf

# NDVI of a part of south-western Oregon (371 x 371 cells), the best-fitting trend already removed
z = tf.load_raster(tf.surface.example_data("normforest"))

metrics.name: Average roughness (Sa)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.range: 0 or more; 0 for a flat surface
metrics.what:
The typical distance of a cell's value from the surface's mean: how rough the surface is, in the surface's own
unit. It is the most used amplitude parameter, simple to read and little affected by a few extreme cells.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value
symbols.\\bar{z}: the mean of the values, \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_k z_k\)

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the roughness of two surfaces in the same unit (the NDVI of two forests, the elevation of two
terrains). It does not tell the shape of the roughness, only its size: pair it with `Ssk` and the spatial metrics
to know whether the roughness comes from peaks or valleys, and how far apart they are.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Root mean square roughness (Sq)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The standard deviation of the surface's values, in the surface's unit. Like Sa it measures how far the values
spread from the mean, but it squares the differences first, so a few high peaks or deep valleys weigh more.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value

metrics.use:
Use it as the spread of the heights, and as the scale that the shape metrics (`Ssk`, `Sku`) are divided by. Sq is at
least as large as Sa, and much larger when there are outliers. Terraflux divides by the number of cells, as
ISO 25178 does; the R package geodiv divides by one less (the sample standard deviation), which differs by a
factor of \(\sqrt{(N-1)/N}\), negligible for a real map.

metrics.name: Skewness (Ssk)
metrics.range: no fixed limits; 0 for a symmetric distribution of values
metrics.what:
Whether the surface's values are balanced around the mean or lean to one side. A negative value means that valleys
(values far below the mean) dominate over peaks, as in a plateau cut by gullies or a canopy with gaps; a positive
value means isolated peaks stand out over a flat floor.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value
symbols.\\mathrm{Sq}: the root mean square roughness, above

metrics.use:
Use it to tell apart surfaces that have the same Sa or Sq but a different shape. It is unitless, so it compares
surfaces in different units. It is sensitive to a few extreme cells, and is defined only when there are more than
two cells with a value. The value of the library is the adjusted one (the correction factor on the right), as the
adjusted Fisher-Pearson coefficient; `adj=False` leaves it out.
